author: Moss, Jessica
title: Aristotle on the Apparent Good: Perception, Phantasia, Thought, and Desire
ocr_confidence: high (clean text-layer PDF; running prose crisp; transliterated Greek in body, polytonic Greek glyphs in quoted passages and footnotes render with transliteration noise but Bekker loci and English are fully legible)
abstract_paraphrase: The 'apparent good' (phainomenon agathon) is to be taken literally: things appear good to us, just as they appear large or small, through phantasia, the quasi-perceptual capacity responsible for dreams, after-images, and optical illusions (EE VII.2 1235b26-29; de Insomniis 460b16-20). An appearance of goodness is a pleasurable, essentially motivating phantasia-representation derived from a prior pleasurable perception, which then grounds thoughts about goodness ('Practical Empiricism'). Chapter 4 applies this to the passions: against the doxastists (Fortenbaugh, Nussbaum 1996, Dow 2009), fear/anger/shame/pity/envy are pleasurable/painful responses to literal evaluative phantasiai, not to beliefs. The passions belong to the non-rational part of the soul (incapable of belief), so for them being-appeared-to IS a default, non-rational acceptance; evaluative beliefs are normal accompaniments (a phantasia 'as of p' standardly triggers the belief that p, Insomn. 461b31-462a2), not the basis. Hence passions can run against belief (the caged man at the precipice; akrasia). Chapter 5 (= Moss 2009 / aes-03) supplies the divergence-cases.

outline.summary: Introduction. Master thesis: take 'apparent' in 'apparent good' literally, on the model of optical appearance (epigraphs EE VII.2 1235b26-29 + Insomn. 460b16-20). Two roles of the apparent good (motivation in general / mistaken motivation) match two roles of phantasia (representing absent objects / misrepresenting them). 'Practical Empiricism': practical thought derives its content from practical perception via phantasia, as theoretical thought derives from perception. Two radical consequences: pleasure central to motivation/virtue; intellect's role restricted. Three-part structure (Part I derive evaluative phantasia; Part II non-rational motivation = passions + akrasia; Part III rational motivation = decision + wish).

Ch. 3 Phantasia and the Apparent Good. (3.1) phantasia specially necessary for locomotion because creatures apprehend goals AS good through it (MA 702a17-19; de An. 432b15-16). (3.2) Minimalist 'basic conception' against Nussbaum/Modrak/Lorenz: phantasia is just 'a movement arising from actual perception' (de An. 428a1-2, 429a1-2), exhaustively given by three claims (arises from perception; independent of present objects; phantasmata similar to aisthemata, so similar effects). (3.3) The crucial similarity is AFFECTIVE: phantasia preserves the pleasurableness/painfulness of perception (MA 701b13-19, 701b33-35, 702a2-7; Rhet. 1370a27-35; Phys. 247a7-14), so a pleasurable desire-inducing phantasia IS an evaluative phantasia, a cognition of something as good = the apparent good (63-64). (3.4) Three relations of phantasia to thought (without / conflicting / agreeing); even practical thought presupposes a corresponding evaluative phantasia from which it takes content (de An. 431a14-17, 432a8-9).

Ch. 4 opens (epigraph: Posidonius fr. 162 on moving the non-rational only by setting before it a picture like a perception). 4.1 Doxastic vs. phantastic accounts of the passions: the Rhetoric's phantasia/phainesthai-laden definitions (Fear = pain from the phantasia of a future evil, Rhet. 1382a21-22) are 'far too quick' an argument; the DOXASTISTS (Fortenbaugh, Nussbaum 1996, Dow 2009) read the appearance-language as non-technical (vividness/subjectivity) and the passions as based on doxa. Moss's two aims: show passions involve LITERAL phantasiai; show this accommodates the pro-belief evidence.

4.2 The passionate part of the soul. Tripartite soul (by relation to logos): the passions are seated in the middle, logos-OBEYING-but-not-exercising part = the pathetikon (Pol. 1254b8), which exercises perception and phantasia but NOT belief (orektikon = aisthetikon = phantastikon: de An. 431a13-14; Insomn. 459a16-17; EE 1219b23). Against Fortenbaugh (2002), who makes it a division of nous on the 'peculiarly human' passages: those contrast only with the nutritive part, and Aristotle plainly grants animals some passions (de An. 403a5-18 clinches the body-involving, non-intellectual status).

4.3 Passions in the Rhetoric. Three essential features of the passion-class: pleasurable/painful; evaluative; the work of phantasia. Argument: (i) all pleasure/pain in perception or quasi-perception (weak-perception passage Rhet. 1370a28-35; Phys. 247a7-14); (ii) passions essentially pleasurable/painful (1378a19-22; EN II.5 1105b21-23; EE II.2 1220b12-14); so they involve perception or phantasia; (iii) passions are directed at NON-PRESENT objects (memory/expectation/'before the eyes' visualization) so phantasia in particular. Anger-as-dreams passage decisive (1378b1-10); pity/shame induced by pro ommaton poiein (1386a29-b7; Cydias 1384b32-35).

4.4 Platonic precedent. Plato makes quasi-perceptual imaginative embellishment a necessary condition of the passions: Philebus scribe-and-painter (hope = vivid painted phantasma of oneself 'beside himself with delight', 39a-40a); Timaeus liver-mirror (rational part reaches appetite only via phantasmata that make a course of action 'look good or bad, the way something can look good or bad in a picture', 71a-d). Strengthens the Aristotelian reading.

4.5 First doxastic objection: the contents of perception (Dow 2009). Objection: passion-representations are propositional and predicate value-properties (a slight, undeserved well-doing) that cannot be perceived. Reply: Aristotle treats perception of common/incidental perceptibles as propositional (de An. 418a21-22, 430b29-30; Sorabji 1996); and value IS literally perceptible (Ch. 2). Decisive: EN VII.6 1149a32-34 contrasts 'logos OR phantasia' as sources of awareness of a slight - belies a doxastic reading; one can have a phantasia OF something AS an insult. Stoics/Epicureans follow in treating value-impressions as perceptual.

4.6 Second doxastic objection: accepting vs. believing (Nussbaum 1996, Dow 2009; cf. Cooper 1996a) - THE pivotal section for the dissertation. (a) phantasia is inert (de An. 427b17-24, the picture-comparison) - Reply: that concerns only the VOLUNTARY 'up-to-us' species; dreams/illusions/Poetics-tragedy do move us; blanket reading contradicts de An. 429a4-8 + MA. (b) passions need ACCEPTANCE not mere appearance - Reply: introduce 'acceptance' as a genus of active assent + passive failure-to-question; for the NON-RATIONAL soul-part there is NO gap between being-appeared-to and accepting, so being subject to an evaluative appearance entails non-rational acceptance = the passion (93). Advantage: passions independent of belief (Hume's caged man; Gendler's alief).

4.7 Aristotle and the Stoics on phantasia, assent, and passion. Stoic frame: all animals have phantasiai; rational creatures assent (synkatathesis -> doxa) or reject; animals 'go with appearances by default'. Impulsive (hormetikai) evaluative phantasiai -> assent -> passion, making Stoic passions rational-only. Striking difference: Aristotelian passions are exactly what the Stoics attribute to ANIMALS and refuse to call passions - default, passive acceptances of appearances (93). This dissolves the second doxastic objection.

4.8 Aristotle and the Stoics on passions, phantasia, and belief. Accommodate the pro-belief evidence via two theses: (a) all thought requires phantasia, so phantasia is NECESSARY for any belief-mediated passion (de An. 432a3-9, 431a14-17; Mem. 449b30-450a9); (b) a phantasia 'as of p' standardly TRIGGERS the belief that p, so phantasia is SUFFICIENT for belief (finger-on-eye proof, Insomn. 461b31-462a2) = proto-Stoic 'appearance-based beliefs' (cf. Sextus AM 7.225-6, restricted). DECLINES the strongly-Stoicizing reading that bases the passion on the belief (Andronicus/Aspasius in EN 44.33-45.10) because it clashes with the non-rationality of the passions. CONCLUSION: passions are based on phantasiai ALONE, but those phantasiai normally prompt corresponding beliefs (round/round analogy, 99). Ch. 5 (= aes-03) gives the divergence-cases (akrasia).

Ch. 5 Akrasia and the Apparent Good = book-form of Moss 2009 (aes-03); NOT re-analyzed. akrasia = conflict between the belief that something is bad and the phantasia that it is good, structurally identical to perceptual illusion; the de Anima III.9-10 account reconciles the struggle and ignorance accounts. Referenced as the source of the passion-vs-belief divergence cases that prove the independence claimed in Ch. 4.

concepts.label: the apparent good (phainomenon agathon) taken literally
concepts.gloss: things appear good as they appear large/small, via phantasia; the master notion of the book, fixed by EE VII.2 1235b26-29 + Insomn. 460b16-20 (Intro xi-xii).

concepts.label: evaluative phantasia (appearance of goodness)
concepts.gloss: a pleasurable, essentially motivating quasi-perceptual representation of an object AS good, derived from a prior pleasurable perception (Ch.3, 63-64); the cognitive basis of all desire and all passion.

concepts.label: Practical Empiricism
concepts.gloss: practical thought derives its content from practical (pleasurable/painful) perception via phantasia, as theoretical thought derives from perception; pleasure the efficient cause of all desire, intellect's role restricted (Intro xiii-xv).

concepts.label: the basic (minimalist) conception of phantasia
concepts.gloss: phantasia is just 'a movement arising from actual perception', a faculty of preserving/reproducing perceptual experience, exhaustively given by three claims; it does NOT interpret or add content (against Nussbaum/Modrak/Lorenz) (3.2, 51-57).

concepts.label: affective preservation: phantasia copies pleasure/pain
concepts.gloss: the crucial similarity between phantasia and perception is affective: a phantasia of an object of pursuit is itself heating/chilling, pleasant/painful, hence itself motivating (MA 701b13-19, 702a2-7; Rhet. 1370a27-35) (3.3).

concepts.label: phantastic account of the passions
concepts.gloss: fear/anger/shame/pity/envy are pleasurable/painful responses to literal evaluative phantasiai (the same quasi-perceptual appearances found in memories and dreams) (Ch.4, 69, 76-84).

concepts.label: doxastic account of the passions (the rival)
concepts.gloss: the view Moss opposes: passions essentially involve belief/doxa, and the Rhetoric's appearance-language is non-technical (vividness/subjectivity); held by Fortenbaugh, Nussbaum 1996, Dow 2009 (4.1, 70).

concepts.label: the passionate part of the soul (pathetikon) is incapable of belief
concepts.gloss: the passions are seated in the logos-obeying-not-exercising middle part = orektikon = aisthetikon = phantastikon (de An. 431a13-14; Insomn. 459a16-17), which exercises perception/phantasia but NOT doxa (4.2, 71-75).

concepts.label: accepting vs. believing (acceptance as a genus)
concepts.gloss: 'acceptance' = genus covering active rational assent + passive failure-to-question; for the non-rational soul-part there is no gap between being-appeared-to and accepting, so emotion requires acceptance but NOT belief (4.6, 90-93). DISSERTATION-PIVOTAL.

concepts.label: non-rational (default) acceptance = the passion itself
concepts.gloss: being subject to an evaluative appearance, for the non-rational part, is a default/automatic/unreflective acceptance which IS or causes the passion (the Stoic 'proto-passion'); fear is the non-rational acceptance of an appearance as terrible (93).

concepts.label: phantasia necessary for thought/belief (thesis a)
concepts.gloss: no thought without a phantasma (de An. 432a3-9, 431a14-17; Mem. 449b30-450a9), so phantasia is a necessary condition even of belief-mediated passions (4.8, 94-96).

concepts.label: phantasia sufficient for belief: appearance-based beliefs (thesis b)
concepts.gloss: a phantasia 'as of p' standardly triggers the belief that p unless rejected (finger-on-eye proof, Insomn. 461b31-462a2); a proto-Stoic account of appearance-based belief (4.8, 96-98).

concepts.label: passions based on phantasia ALONE, belief a normal accompaniment
concepts.gloss: Moss's reconciling conclusion: passions rest on phantasiai alone (hence non-rational, hence can conflict with belief), but those phantasiai normally prompt corresponding evaluative beliefs (round/round analogy, 98-99).

concepts.label: passions independent of belief (recalcitrance)
concepts.gloss: one can have a passion against one's belief (Hume's caged man at the precipice; cf. Gendler's alief; akrasia), which the doxastist must deny but common sense affirms (94).

concepts.label: value is literally perceptible / propositional perception
concepts.gloss: Aristotle treats perception of common/incidental perceptibles as propositional and value as literally perceptible; intellect may expand the perceptual range (perceiving insults as insults like roses as roses) (4.5, 87-90).

concepts.label: 'before the eyes' (pro ommaton poiein) as the signature of phantasia
concepts.gloss: orators induce pity/shame by vivid quasi-perceptual visualization 'before the eyes' (de An. 427b18-19; Mem. 450a5; Insomn. 458b20); we induce passions in ourselves the same way (4.3, 83-84).

concepts.label: Stoic phantasia + assent (synkatathesis) as interpretive lens
concepts.gloss: Aristotle's view is more Stoic-like than recognized: Aristotelian passions are what the Stoics ascribe to animals and refuse to call passions (default acceptances), not rational assents (4.7, 92-94).

concepts.label: Platonic precedent (Philebus painter; Timaeus liver-mirror)
concepts.gloss: Plato makes quasi-perceptual evaluative images a necessary condition of the passions (Phil. 39a-40a; Tim. 71a-d), anticipating Aristotle (4.4, 85-87).

concepts.label: two-tier architecture (non-rational basis + doxastic overlay)
concepts.gloss: Moss's thesis-(b) is already a two-level picture: a non-rational phantastic basis plus a normal doxastic accompaniment - the template the dissertation can adopt and then argue the overlay is constitutive for civic emotions.

concepts.label: passions affect judgments (kriseis) without being judgments
concepts.gloss: appeal-to-passion sways jurors' kriseis because passions' underlying phantasiai trigger beliefs; but anger 'does not already entail a judgment' (Rhet. 1378a19-22; 1354a24-26) (4.8, 99).

readings.thesis: The apparent good is a literal quasi-perceptual phantasia-appearance, on the model of optical appearance (the sun a foot wide); phantasia and belief reside in different parts of the soul.
Phantasia is minimalist - just 'a movement arising from actual perception' that preserves and reproduces perceptual experience (incl. its affective component); it does NOT interpret or add content.
A pleasurable, desire-inducing phantasia IS an evaluative phantasia - a cognition of something as good; this is the analysis of the apparent good and the basis of all desire.
The passions are based on LITERAL phantasiai, not on beliefs (the phantastic account), against the doxastists.
The passions are seated in the non-rational part of the soul, which exercises perception and phantasia but is incapable of belief; therefore their cognition must be non-rational.
Accepting vs. believing: emotion requires acceptance, but for the non-rational soul-part being-appeared-to IS a default, non-rational acceptance, so emotion does NOT require belief.

Passions are based on phantasiai alone, but those phantasiai normally trigger corresponding evaluative beliefs (phantasia necessary AND sufficient for belief); so passions correlate with beliefs without being functions of belief, and can in special cases conflict with them.
Passions are independent of belief: one can feel a passion against one's evaluative belief (the recalcitrance / akrasia cases), which the doxastist must deny.

Aristotle's passions are NOT Stoic rational assents but precisely the default, passive acceptances of appearances the Stoics attribute to animals and refuse to call passions; Aristotle declines the strongly-Stoicizing belief-based reading.

aristotle_loci.role: KEYSTONE epigraph: the desired is the good or apparent good; the pleasant appears good to some who do not believe it; phantasia and belief not in the same part of the soul
KEYSTONE epigraph: the sun appears a foot wide though contradicted; the judging faculty != the phantasma faculty (optical model of the apparent good)
the sun appears a foot wide though believed larger than the earth; Cooper's 'nonepistemic appearance' (4.6); phantasia != doxa
definition: phantasia is that in virtue of which a phantasma comes to be for us
phantasia = 'a movement arising from actual perception' (the basic conception, 3.2)
phantasia a movement similar to the perception it arises from; one does and undergoes many things in accordance with it
because phantasiai remain and are similar to perceptions, animals do many things in accordance with them; phantasia can induce action/emotion (cited vs the inert-phantasia reading)
phantasia does not arise without perception; thinking is part phantasia, part supposition (hypolepsis) - the proto-Stoic passages (4.8)
phantasia 'up to us' / believing not; imagining something terrible like seeing it in a picture (the inertness objection, 4.6) - confined to the VOLUNTARY species
animals lack belief because they lack the conviction (pistis) that follows from logos; 'conviction' as the Stoic-assent analogue
the orektikon is the same as (different only in being from) the aisthetikon - founds the identity pathetikon=aisthetikon=phantastikon (4.2)
no thought without a phantasma; the soul affirms/denies good/bad and flees/pursues; phantasia necessary for all (incl. practical) thought (thesis a, 4.8; 3.4)
pleasurable perception essentially entails desire / perceives the good (3.3; basis of evaluative perception)
the object of desire moves by being thought or represented by phantasia; desire requires phantasia (the necessity-of-phantasia passages)
locomotion is always for the sake of something and is with phantasia or desire (3.1)
perception of common/incidental perceptibles is propositional ('that the white thing is a man') - answers the propositional-content objection (4.5)
the pathe (anger, fear, pity, daring, etc.) are all 'with the body'; 'in general perceive' arguably identifies passions as species of perception (4.2)
the finger-on-eye proof: the doubled finger is BELIEVED double unless one notices/rejects the appearance - phantasia standardly triggers belief (thesis b, 4.8)
phantasia-mechanism: aisthema/phantasma; phantasmata remain after perceiving and are similar to perceptions (3.2)
phantasia 'places before the eyes'; thought and phantasia can contradict one another (the conflict-relation, 3.4)
memory is an operation of phantasia; phantasma like a painting/seal-imprint; 'places before the eyes'; we think universals by inspecting a particular phantasma

phantasiai/perceptions/thoughts alter the parts; phantasia 'has the power of the actual things'; heating/chilling attend the phantasia of objects of pursuit/avoidance; the affective-preservation evidence (3.3, 4.6)
Fear is a pain/disturbance arising from the phantasia of a destructive or painful future evil (the paradigm phantastic definition)
general definition: the passions are those things on account of which, by change, people differ in their judgments (kriseis), attended by pleasure/pain
definitions of anger/shame/confidence/pity/indignation/envy/rivalry, all phantasia- or phainesthai-laden
the phantasia in anger produces pleasure 'just as the phantasia that occurs in dreams' - the most unequivocal technical use (4.3)
the 'weak perception' passage (phantasia = weak perception; pleasures of memory/expectation); pleasures of anger/appetite/love/victory/honor attributed to phantasia (3.3, 4.3)
inducing pity/shame by 'putting before the eyes' (pro ommaton); Cydias on Samos (the visualization evidence, 4.3)
things causing pain are perceptible; the 'think/oiesthai' passages doxastists cite (handled in 4.5-4.8)
passions 'prepare the judge' / affect kriseis in lawcourts - passions influence but are not themselves judgments (4.8)
'logos OR phantasia has shown that something was hubris or a slight' - 'belies a doxastic interpretation' (4.5, key anti-doxastic text)
the tripartite/bipartite soul; the passionate part obeys but does not exercise logos; the struggle picture (Ch.5)
the passions are pleasure/pain-attended; character is a disposition to feel them; passions body-yoked, not divine/intellectual
the perceptive-and-desiderative part crucial to virtue; 'peculiarly human' passages (answered vs Fortenbaugh); passions attended by perceptual pleasure/pain
in akrasia/enkrateia the rational and appetitive are so opposed one is 'forced/compelled' by the other (the struggle account; Ch.5)
the pathetikon meros (passionate part); natural slaves obey passions; humans 'have perception of the good and bad, just and unjust' (value-perception, 4.5 n.35)
the apparent fine = object of appetite vs the real fine = object of wish (the apparent-good corpus pattern, cited across Part I)
the pleasures/pains of memory and expectation arise from perceptibles; pleasure an alteration of the aisthetikon (3.3, 4.3)
we feel genuine pity/fear at theatrical representations - evidence phantasia/representation can induce real passions (4.6)

tensions.desc: Substantial Rhetoric + de An. III.3 evidence that passions correlate with beliefs (dokein/oiesthai; 'when we believe something terrible we are affected') seems to favor the doxastists; Moss reconciles via theses (a)+(b): phantasia necessary AND sufficient for belief, so passions rest on phantasia alone while normally triggering belief (4.8).

de An. III.3 427b21-24 says imagining something terrible is inert (like a picture), seeming to deny phantasia can move us; Moss confines this to the VOLUNTARY 'up-to-us' species and notes the residual difficulty, deferring full treatment to Ch.6.

Moss's phantastic, non-doxastic account of the PASSIONS (by name) is the centerpiece rival to the dissertation's doxa-requirement; her wedge is that the passionate part is incapable of belief (4.2), which the dissertation must show does not bind the higher civic emotions.

The accepting-vs-believing distinction (4.6) shows 'emotion requires taking-things-to-be-so' is satisfied by sub-doxastic default acceptance, NOT full doxa; the dissertation's 'doxa = involuntary positive taking-as-true' must require the ACTIVE/rational species of acceptance Moss reserves for belief.

Moss's thesis-(b) is itself a two-tier picture (non-rational phantastic basis + normal doxastic overlay); the dissertation can adopt it and argue the overlay is constitutive for civic emotions - contesting Moss's round/round separability analogy (99).

Moss argues animals genuinely have passions on phantastic grounds (4.2, 4.7), against Konstan/Fortenbaugh/Stoic 'only analogous'; the dissertation's animal-exclusion claim must target only the rational/doxastic civic-emotion overlay.

dissertation_hooks.T1-2: PRIMARY rival, Ch.4 the centerpiece; the passions on the phantastic (non-doxastic) model, by name, vs Fortenbaugh/Dow; supports two-tier reconciliation (phantastic lower tier / doxa higher tier)
dissertation_hooks.doxa-concept: accepting-vs-believing: acceptance < belief; default non-rational acceptance satisfies 'taking-as-true' without doxa - the deflationary rival to 'doxa = positive taking-as-true'
dissertation_hooks.two-tier: Moss's phantasia-necessary-and-sufficient-for-belief (theses a+b) IS a non-rational-basis + doxastic-overlay architecture; round/round separability analogy is the hinge to contest
dissertation_hooks.animal-pathos: animals have genuine (non-rational) pathe on phantastic grounds - the dissertation concedes the basal pathe, reserves doxa-involving civic emotions for the rational overlay
dissertation_hooks.T1-4: the apparent good is phantasia-based and can represent absent/never-perceived objects, so emotions toward non-realizable goods need only an evaluative phantasia (grief/wish material deferred to Part III/Ch.7)
